meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Hands-on learning with step-by-step guidance. Each exercise builds on the previous. All concepts from the session are coded. Banking/finance examples used for context.

objectives: Set up Java development environment and write/run your first Java program
Declare variables using all 8 primitive types with appropriate contexts
Apply arithmetic, relational, logical, and ternary operators
Implement all flow control structures: if/else, switch, for, while, do-while, break, continue
Create, populate, sort, and search arrays using the Arrays utility class
Apply Java naming conventions and best practices in all code
prerequisites: IntelliJ IDEA (Community Edition) or VS Code with Java Extension
Git installed and GitHub account created

exercises.title: Your First Java Program — Hello, Software Engineer!
exercises.objective: Understand the structure of a Java program, compile and run it, and understand the role of JVM/JDK/JRE.
exercises.scenario: You just joined RoboBank's technology team as a fresher. Your first task: set up your Java environment and write a program that introduces you to the team.
instructions: Step 1: Open your IDE and create a new Java project called 'Day01_JavaFundamentals'
Step 2: Create a new Java class named 'HelloEngineer' inside the project's src folder
Step 3: Type (don't copy-paste!) the starter code below
Step 4: Run the program (Shift+F10 in IntelliJ, or F5 in VS Code)
Step 5: Open a terminal and locate the compiled .class file: it should be in 'out/' or 'build/' folder
Step 6: From the terminal, try: javac HelloEngineer.java → java HelloEngineer
Step 7: Modify the output to include YOUR name and YOUR city
Checkpoint: Can you explain to a classmate what javac does vs what java does?
exercises.expected_output:
Hello from RoboBank Tech Team!
I am: [Your Name]
Based in: [Your City]
Java version I'm using: 17.0.x

--- Java Platform Architecture ---
JDK  = JRE + Development Tools (javac, javadoc, jar)
JRE  = JVM + Standard Class Libraries
JVM  = Executes .class bytecode | Platform-specific
WORA = Write Once, Run Anywhere!
hints: If you get 'class not found': make sure the filename matches the class name exactly (case-sensitive!)
If you see a .class file in a folder — that's the bytecode! Open it in Notepad to see it's not readable — that's the JVM's job to understand it.
Each System.out.println() is one statement. Every statement ends with a semicolon.
reflection_questions: What is the difference between a .java file and a .class file?
Why can the same .class file run on both Windows and Linux?
What would happen if you renamed HelloEngineer.java to Hello.java without changing the class name?
exercises.debugging_task: Try removing the semicolon from one of the println statements and recompile. What error do you get? Read the error message carefully — what does it tell you?

exercises.title: Primitive Data Types — Bank Account Record
exercises.objective: Use all 8 Java primitive types in a meaningful context and understand their sizes, ranges, and appropriate use cases.
exercises.scenario: Model a bank account record using the most appropriate Java primitive type for each field. This is the foundation of data modeling in any banking system.
instructions: Step 1: Create a new Java class called 'BankAccountRecord' in the same project
Step 2: Declare one variable for each of the 8 primitive types (see starter code)
Step 3: Print each variable using System.out.printf for formatted output
Step 4: Add a TASK comment where indicated and complete each task
Step 5: Run and verify your output matches the expected output
Step 6: EXPERIMENT — what happens when you assign 200 to a byte? What error do you get?
Step 7: EXPERIMENT — what does Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 print? Can you explain why?
exercises.expected_output:
========== Bank Account Details ==========
Account Number  : 9876543210
Branch Code     : 1042
Transaction Count: 1500
KYC Status      : 2 (0=Pending, 1=Submitted, 2=Verified)
Balance         : 150000.75
Interest Rate   : 8.5%
Account Type    : S
Is Active       : true

========== Primitive Ranges ==========
Byte max     : 127
Short max    : 32767
Int max      : 2147483647
Long max     : 9223372036854775807

========== Overflow Experiment ==========
Integer.MAX_VALUE     : 2147483647
Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 : -2147483648

========== Floating-Point Precision ==========
0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004

hints: The 'L' suffix in 9876543210L tells Java this is a long literal (without 'L', Java reads integer literals as int, causing compile error for numbers > 2.1 billion)
Underscores in numbers (1_500, 1_50_000.75) are allowed from Java 7+ — they only affect readability, not the value
BigDecimal constructor takes a String argument, NOT a double. new BigDecimal(0.1) still has precision issues!
reflection_questions: Why is int insufficient for storing phone numbers? Which type would you use?
A bank transaction might store an amount like ₹99,99,999.99 — which type(s) would you consider and why?
What would happen if a banking system used int (not long) for account balances and a customer had ₹22 crore in their account?
exercises.debugging_task: Deliberately introduce this bug and observe the error: byte buggy = 200; What does the compiler say? Change it to short — does it work?

exercises.title: Operators — Interest & EMI Calculator
exercises.objective: Apply all major operator types: arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, increment/decrement, and ternary to build real calculation logic.
exercises.scenario: RoboBank needs a quick interest and loan eligibility calculator. You'll build it using Java operators.
instructions: Step 1: Create class 'OperatorsDemo' in your project
Step 2: Implement each section of the starter code, replacing TODO comments
Step 3: Run and verify all outputs
Step 4: Experiment with changing values and predict the output BEFORE running
Step 5: Complete the CHALLENGE at the bottom

exercises.title: Flow Control — ATM Simulator
exercises.objective: Implement all flow control structures (if/else, switch, for, while, do-while, break, continue) in a realistic ATM simulation.
exercises.scenario: Build a simplified ATM simulator for RoboBank. It validates PIN (do-while), processes transactions (switch), handles withdrawals (if/else), and generates a mini-statement (for loop).
instructions: Step 1: Create class 'ATMSimulator' and type the starter code
Step 2: Complete all TODO sections — do NOT skip any
Step 3: Run with the test data provided (pinAttempts array simulates user input)
Step 4: Change the test data to test edge cases: wrong PIN 3 times, insufficient balance, zero amount
Step 5: Add a new transaction type: 'B' for Balance Inquiry (print the balance)
Step 6: CHALLENGE: Add a minimum balance check — don't allow withdrawal if balance would go below ₹1000

hints: do-while checks condition AFTER the body — guarantees at least one execution. Perfect for 'show prompt, then validate' patterns.
switch falls through unless you use break. In our switch: break exits the switch; to exit the outer for loop from inside case 'Q', use a boolean flag: boolean quit = false; then check while (!quit).
Math.abs(-5000) = 5000. Useful for converting negative debit amounts to positive for display.
reflection_questions: Why is do-while more appropriate than while for the PIN authentication loop?
What would happen with 'break' inside the switch case 'Q' — does it exit the for loop or just the switch?
Can you rewrite the for-each loop in Section 3 as a traditional for loop? Which is cleaner?
exercises.debugging_task: Add this code and observe: simulate a card being blocked. Set simulatedPINs = {9999, 8888, 7777} (all wrong). Does your card-blocked logic trigger? What output do you see?

exercises.title: Arrays — Branch Performance Dashboard
exercises.objective: Create, traverse, sort, search, and analyze arrays. Use the Arrays utility class. Practice both traditional for loops and enhanced for-each loops.
exercises.scenario: RoboBank has 6 branches across India. Build a performance dashboard that analyzes deposit amounts, sorts branches, finds top/bottom performers, and generates a formatted report.
instructions: Step 1: Create class 'BranchDashboard'
Step 2: Implement all sections — each section teaches a new array concept
Step 3: Run and verify output
Step 4: MODIFICATION — Add a 7th branch 'Pune' with ₹95,00,000. Update the array. Do you need to change anything else?
Step 5: CHALLENGE at the end — implement without using Arrays.sort()

hints: Always initialize max/min to the first element (deposits[0]), NOT to 0. If all values were negative, 0 would incorrectly be the 'max'.
Arrays.copyOf() creates a new array with the same elements — so sorting the copy doesn't affect the original array and its index relationship with the branches array.
System.out.printf with %,.2f adds comma separators and 2 decimal places. The 'n' after the % is the flag for thousand separator (locale-specific).
reflection_questions: Why do we initialize maxDeposit = deposits[0] instead of maxDeposit = 0? When would maxDeposit = 0 give a wrong answer?
Why must we use Arrays.copyOf() before sorting if we want to find the branch name later?
Without Arrays.toString(), what does System.out.println(deposits) print? Try it — understand why the output looks strange.
exercises.debugging_task: Add this code: double[] emptyArr = new double[0]; System.out.println(emptyArr[0]); — what exception do you get? How would you safely handle an empty array before finding max/min?

exercises.title: Capstone Lab — Mini Bank Statement Generator
exercises.objective: Combine ALL Day 1 concepts in a single integrated program: primitives, operators, flow control, arrays, and best practices to build a complete mini banking application.
exercises.scenario: Build a mini bank statement generator for RoboBank. It processes an array of transactions, categorizes them, computes running balance, flags large transactions, and prints a formatted statement. This represents the kind of real code you'll write as a Java developer.
instructions: Step 1: Create class 'BankStatementGenerator'
Step 2: Implement all sections — this is your Day 1 integration test
Step 3: Run and match expected output
Step 4: Add a feature: also count how many transactions are above ₹20,000
Step 5: Git commit your work: 'Day 1: Java fundamentals complete - primitives, operators, control flow, arrays'
hints: String.format("₹%,.2f", amount) formats a number with rupee symbol, comma separators, and 2 decimals.
Math.abs(txnAmt) gives the absolute value — useful to track debit amounts as positive numbers.
To print top 3 from sorted (ascending) array: loop from length-1 down to length-3.
reflection_questions: This program uses int, double, boolean, char, and String. Which Java primitive types did we NOT use here — and can you add a use case for each?
Why do we use static final constants instead of inline magic numbers?
If you had 10,000 transactions, would this approach still work? What would you change?
exercises.debugging_task: Intentionally remove the Math.abs() from totalDebit. What happens to the total debit amount? Why? This demonstrates why absolute value handling is critical in financial calculations.

submission_instructions: After completing all 6 exercises, push your project to GitHub. Commit message: 'Day 1 Lab Complete: Java fundamentals - primitives, operators, control flow, arrays, best practices'. Add a README.md explaining what each class does.
